Sponsored by



Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg News



The U.S. economy keeps powering through inflation, tariffs and higher borrowing costs, defying a run-up in Treasury yields and a Fed rate increase. That has the bond market spooked.

The usual economic brakes aren’t slowing growth, hiring or an AI investment boom that looks to be unstoppable. To some, AI’s potential returns seem so bright that even steep interest rates won’t slow down tech companies’ investments.

The growth outlook helps explain  the current predicament in the bond market. [https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/us-economy-bond-market-0bfda8b3]

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

Planning & Investing               The Peptide Boom That Isn’t About Your Muscles

The real opportunity is pill-form peptides that could hit  big pharma’s most profitable franchises [https://www.wsj.com/health/pharma/the-peptide-boom-that-isnt-about-your-muscles-4aa63e38].

The Rise of the Almost-Premium Credit Card

Higher annual fees on top-tier cards have led to  a reshuffling of the market [https://www.wsj.com/personal-finance/credit/the-rise-of-the-almost-premium-credit-card-f6d22ebd], with cards just below that level targeting the not-quite-rich enough.

Market Talk               

From  Dow Jones Newswires [https://www.dowjones.com/professional/newswires/]



Scotiabank remains bullish on Canada's banks. It reckons Prime Minister Carney's Building Canada Strong plan could help keep foreign capital flows positive both within the financial sector and across the Canadian market more broadly, which would provide further support to TSX-listed bank valuations. The big banks are currently expected to deliver slightly more than 10% EPS growth in 2027, with potential upside, and recent bank management comments on capital markets activity remains positive, Scotiabank says. It argues that even if bank valuation multiples remain near current levels, solid earnings plus the sector's dividend yield should still offer attractive return potential. (Robb Stewart, robb.stewart@wsj.com)

Climbing energy prices means the Bank of England is now on course to tighten policy, Morgan Stanley's Bruna Skarica and Fabio Bassanin say in a note. They change their BOE call to two quarterly interest-rate hikes in November and February. "While we still think--and with a decent degree of conviction--that any signs of an improvement in the supply in oil and refined products would leave the BOE on hold from here, it is challenging to maintain a prolonged hold as a modal call amid the recent Middle East newsflow," they say. The only catalyst for even stronger tightening would be a materially fiscally loose and inflationary budget announced next month, they say. (Edward Frankl, edward.frankl@wsj.com)

Learn More  [http://pubads.g.doubleclick.net/gampad/clk?id=7429927158&iu=/2]

Barron's Advisor               The Number of Student Loans in Default Is Bad and Likely to Get Worse

A federal overhaul of student loan repayment plans and an end of Covid-Era relief programs have created confusion and distrust among borrowers that  experts expect will lead to increasing defaults [https://www.barrons.com/advisor/articles/student-loan-default-e34aeba9].

Did Fake Comments Boost Proposal to Put Alternative Investments in Retirement Plans? Lawmakers Call for Probe

Three members of Congress are asking the Justice Department, FBI, and Labor Department to look into  nearly 12,000 apparently fake comments [https://www.barrons.com/advisor/articles/labor-department-alternative-investments-retirement-plans-fake-comments-probe-43c77675] in favor of the controversial proposal.

Business & Practice               AI Is a Regulator’s Nightmare

There is no template [https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/ai-is-a-regulators-nightmare-39d7fa7a] for a technology that is both immensely beneficial and deeply dangerous.

Impact Investing               Climate Tech VCs Zero In on Powering AI Instead of Cutting Carbon Emissions

Climate-tech venture investors don’t talk much these days about climate change. What they are focused on now is artificial intelligence and the  energy needed to power data centers [https://www.wsj.com/pro/venture-capital/climate-tech-vcs-zero-in-on-powering-ai-instead-of-cutting-carbon-emissions-cd5a4e32], much like the rest of the investment world.

Talking Points               Portland Real Estate Is Such a Mess That All Housing Is Affordable Housing

Rarely has the Oregon city seen  such a narrow price gap [https://www.wsj.com/real-estate/portland-real-estate-is-such-a-mess-that-all-housing-is-affordable-housing-26bbea6a] between market-rate and affordable units.

Travel & Lifestyle               How an Iced Coffee in a Job Interview Sparked a Raging Etiquette Debate            

Getty Images



A simple question about the drink has highlighted shifting expectations of professionalism. Recruiters and career coaches have  some advice [https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/careers/how-an-iced-coffee-in-a-job-interview-sparked-a-raging-etiquette-debate-46ffb767].

Colleges Once Saw High Tuition as a Sign of Quality. Now They’re Slashing Prices

As more families  balk at costs [https://www.wsj.com/us-news/education/college-tuition-cuts-costs-financial-aid-38e749df], some schools are starting to make changes.
